note: Original classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an object can be used as a musical instrument.
questions.prompt: During an assembly rehearsal, a pupil uses a wooden block to play a planned rhythm. Explain how the same block can be a classroom object during one lesson and a musical instrument during rehearsal.
questions.answer: In rehearsal the pupil deliberately uses the block to make and organise sounds in a rhythm. The same block may serve another purpose in an ordinary lesson.
questions.explanation: Musical use depends on how the sound is produced and used within an activity.

markingGuide.description: Connects the produced sound to the planned musical rhythm.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify an electrophone by how it generates its musical signal.
questions.prompt: A classroom keyboard has no strings. Its keys tell a processor which note to generate, and a speaker plays the resulting signal. Which classification best fits this instrument?
questions.explanation: The musical signal originates electronically. The speaker makes that signal audible.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify a chordophone and explain the role of its resonator.
questions.prompt: A pupil plucks an acoustic guitar string. The hollow body helps the note carry through the room. Name the instrument class and explain why the hollow body does not change that classification.
questions.answer: The guitar is a chordophone because the plucked string is the primary vibrating source. The hollow body helps transfer the vibration to the air.
questions.explanation: A resonator can strengthen the audible sound while the string remains the source used for classification.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the vibrating string as the primary sound source.
Explains the body’s role in resonance or sound radiation.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify leno weaving by the crossing of warp threads.
questions.prompt: Using a magnifier, a pupil sees pairs of lengthwise threads cross between successive crosswise threads. Which weave does this feature indicate?
questions.explanation: In a basic leno structure, paired warp threads cross and help hold the weft in place.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why crossed warp pairs can help stabilise an open weave.
questions.prompt: A textile sample has wide gaps between its crosswise yarns. Along each row, neighbouring lengthwise yarns cross so that the crosswise yarn is held between them. Explain how this arrangement can keep the gaps more regular during gentle handling.
questions.answer: The crossed warp pairs grip the weft yarn. This helps limit weft movement, so the open spaces are less likely to close up unevenly.
questions.explanation: An open weave has fewer closely packed crossings to support its spacing. Crossing the warp pairs adds a way to hold the weft in position.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the crossed lengthwise threads as warp.
Explains how the crossed warp pair holds a crosswise yarn or weft.
Links reduced weft movement to more regular spacing.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge of a woven sample to identify warp and weft.
questions.prompt: The teacher gives each group a cloth sample with one original woven side edge and three cut edges. How could the pupils use the original edge to label the two thread directions?
questions.answer: Follow the original woven side edge. Warp runs parallel to it and weft runs across the width at right angles to it.
questions.explanation: A woven side edge runs along the length of the cloth. The crosswise yarns travel across the width.

markingGuide.description: Uses the original woven side edge as the reference.
Identifies the parallel direction as warp.
Identifies the crosswise direction as weft.
